pedagogy.summary: Proportional relationships are represented with double number lines (two parallel scales aligned at 0), ratio tables, and coordinate graphs — and the defining graphical signature is a STRAIGHT LINE THROUGH THE ORIGIN. The representational skills are (1) plotting proportional pairs and drawing that line, (2) explaining WHY it must pass through (0,0) — because zero of one quantity means zero of the other — and (3) reading off an unknown value from the line or table (if 3 kg costs £6, find 5 kg). The key idea to build is that the three representations show the SAME constant multiplier: the gap between rungs on a double number line, the column multiplier in a ratio table, and the gradient of the line are one and the same. The persistent error is thinking any straight line (or any rising graph) shows proportion, ignoring the origin.
bestPractices: Connect the three representations explicitly — double number line, ratio table, and graph — as views of one constant multiplier, moving between them on the same example.
Foreground the origin: ask 'what does it cost for 0 kg?' so pupils reason that a proportional graph MUST pass through (0,0), and use that as a test.
Align double number lines at 0 and keep the scales consistent, so equivalent ratios sit at matching positions.
Read unknowns both by scaling on the table/number line and by reading off the graph, checking the two agree.
Contrast a proportional line (through origin) with a straight line that misses the origin (e.g. a fixed charge plus a rate) so 'straight' alone is not mistaken for 'proportional'.
keyRepresentations: Double number line (two parallel scales aligned at 0)
Ratio table with a constant column multiplier
Coordinate graph: straight line through the origin (gradient = the rate)
Overlay contrasting a through-origin line with a not-through-origin line
commonMisconceptions: Thinking any straight line — or any rising graph — shows direct proportion, ignoring whether it passes through the origin.
Not aligning the double number line at 0, so equivalent ratios don't correspond.
Reading a graph as isolated points and being unable to interpolate an unknown, or swapping the axes when reading off.
Believing the graph need not start at (0,0) — missing that zero of one quantity means zero of the other.

learn.summary: Pupils aged 11–14 learn to represent direct proportion across three linked views — a double number line (two parallel scales aligned at 0), a ratio table in which every kg entry is multiplied by the same constant to give its £ entry, and a coordinate graph whose signature is a STRAIGHT LINE THROUGH THE ORIGIN. The core insight is that the factor linking each pair of matching marks on the double number line (e.g. 1 kg ↔ £2, 3 kg ↔ £6), the kg-to-£ multiplier in each pair in the table, and the gradient of the line (£ per kg) are ONE AND THE SAME constant multiplier. Learners plot proportional pairs and draw the line, explain why it must pass through (0,0) (zero of one quantity means zero of the other), and read off unknowns (if 3 kg costs £6, find 5 kg → £10). The persistent error to confront is treating any straight or rising line as proportional while ignoring the origin.

activities.title: Linked board: one rate, three views that move together
feedback: If a drawn line misses (0,0), ask 'what does it cost for 0 kg?' — it must be £0, so the line has to start at the origin.
If the double number line is not aligned at 0, highlight that equivalent ratios then fail to sit at matching positions; realign at 0.
If axes are swapped when reading off, prompt: read UP from the weight on the x-axis to the line, then ACROSS to the cost on the y-axis.
When the fixed-charge toggle lifts the line off the origin, name it: still straight, but no longer proportional because 0 kg no longer costs £0.
activities.rationale: Plotting pairs, drawing the line, and reading off unknowns are direct-manipulation tasks; moving between the three views on one example is intended to make the shared multiplier concrete, and the fixed-charge contrast separates 'straight' from 'proportional'. Live linking and dragging are offered as examples of how to make the shared multiplier visible, not as the only possible medium.
sourceClaims: A directly proportional relationship graphs as a straight line through the origin; properties include that doubling one quantity doubles the other and that if one quantity is zero the other is zero.

Pupils should use double number lines and ratio tables, and recognise that proportional relationships are represented by straight-line graphs through the origin, relating the multiplicative relationship to linear functions.
learnerActions: Enter or accept a rate such as 3 kg → £6 and watch a ratio table, a double number line, and a coordinate graph populate for the SAME example.
Plot the proportional pairs on the graph and draw the line; confirm it passes through the origin.
Drag a point to 5 kg and read £10 simultaneously on the table, the number line, and the graph.

Point to where the constant '×2' appears in each view: the gradient of the line (£2 per kg), the multiplier from each kg entry to its £ entry in the table (3 → 6, 5 → 10), and the factor linking each pair of matching marks on the double number line (1 kg ↔ £2, 3 kg ↔ £6).
Flip a 'fixed charge' toggle (e.g. add a standing £2) and observe the whole line lift OFF the origin while staying perfectly straight; state whether it is still proportional and why not.
activities.intendedInsight: All three representations encode the SAME constant multiplier, and the origin — not mere straightness — is the test of proportionality.

activities.title: Annotated proportion graph: reveal the origin, the rate, and a read-off
feedback: If the learner calls the not-through-origin line proportional, return to the origin: at 0 kg the fixed-charge line already costs £2, so it fails the origin test.
If the rate is misread, trace one unit along x and read the matching rise on y to recover the constant multiplier.
activities.rationale: A proportion graph is largely a fixed object; annotating it with tap-to-reveal on origin, gradient, and read-off, plus a contrasting line, is intended to rehearse the recognition cues at low cost. A fixed image here cannot be freely manipulated but can still surface these cues for inspection; it complements rather than replaces the interactive board.
sourceClaims: A directly proportional relationship graphs as a straight line through the origin; properties include that doubling one quantity doubles the other and that if one quantity is zero the other is zero.
learnerActions: Examine a proportion graph and reveal, at the origin, that 'at 0 kg, cost is £0'.
Reveal along the line the constant multiplier (the rate, e.g. £2/kg).
Reveal at a chosen point its read-off (e.g. 5 kg → £10).
Compare a companion line that is straight but does NOT pass through the origin (a fixed £2 charge plus £2/kg) and decide, with reasons, that it is not proportional.
activities.intendedInsight: The recognition cues of a proportional graph are the origin crossing and a single constant rate; a straight line that misses the origin is a direct counterexample to 'straight means proportional'.

activities.title: Identify, read, and produce proportional lines
feedback: If a produced line misses (0,0), it is the key discriminator: recognition alone will not place the line; re-anchor using 'at 0 kg, cost £0'.
If an unknown is only found when the weight is an already-plotted point, stress that the line gives a value for EVERY weight, so interpolate between plotted points.
If axes are swapped during read-off, label both axes first, then read up-then-across.

If a £2/kg line is drawn as if it were separate from the given line, point out that equal rates give the SAME line through the origin; a genuinely different rate (e.g. £1/kg through (3,3)) gives a shallower distinct line.
activities.rationale: Identifying the proportional graph, reading off values, matching a table to a line, and drawing a new line are cleanly assessable, with 'any straight line' and axis-swap as sharp distractors. The draw step elicits independent construction, which recognition-only items do not.
sourceClaims: Pupils should use double number lines and ratio tables, and recognise that proportional relationships are represented by straight-line graphs through the origin, relating the multiplicative relationship to linear functions.
learnerActions: Choose which of several graphs shows direct proportion, where a straight not-through-origin line is a deliberate trap.
Given a ratio table, plot the points and draw the matching line through the origin.
Read an unknown off a line through (3,6) (e.g. find the cost of 5 kg → £10), stating which axis you read up from and which you read across to.

On the same axes, DRAW a line for a DIFFERENT fruit's price: note that a £2/kg fruit would COINCIDE with the given £2/kg line through (3,6), whereas a shallower £1/kg line passes through (3,3) — and check your line is anchored at the origin.
activities.intendedInsight: Interpreting a point, interpolating an unknown, and independently producing an origin-anchored line together show whether the learner sees the graph as a constant-multiplier relationship rather than a picture.

constraints: Multiple-choice identification and tap-to-reveal items assess or rehearse recognition of cues; they do not by themselves elicit the independent production of an origin-anchored line, so include a draw/plot task for full mastery.
An annotated fixed graph cannot be freely manipulated; pair it with a task where learners plot, drag, or draw so the constant multiplier is explored, not just viewed.
Always keep double number lines aligned at 0 and scales consistent, or equivalent ratios will not correspond.
When introducing the fixed-charge contrast, state the setup explicitly (e.g. £2 standing charge plus £2/kg) so learners attribute the lifted line to the non-zero start, not to a changed rate.

When asking learners to draw a 'different' line, ensure the chosen rate is genuinely different from any line already on the axes (£1/kg, not £2/kg, against a given £2/kg line), so the task is coherent.

In-role dialogue and 3D manipulation were judged poor fits here: the relationship is inherently 2D (two quantities, one plane), and drawing/reading a graph is a visual-spatial task; these are design judgements for this topic, not universal rules.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic and geometry: at £2/kg, 3 kg → £6 and 5 kg → £10 are consistent; a £1/kg line through the origin passes through (3,3); the fixed-charge example (£2 + £2/kg) correctly gives £2 at 0 kg and so misses the origin. The original's note that a £2/kg drawn line coincides with the given (3,6) line has been preserved and the 'different rate' wording kept coherent (£1/kg used as the genuinely different, shallower line).

The source claims support the mathematical signature (straight line through the origin; zero maps to zero; use of double number lines and ratio tables) but do not establish the comparative efficacy of any particular interface (linked board, tap-to-reveal, drag). Efficacy of specific media is not asserted; medium wording has been kept to proposed/intended.
The original judgement that conversation and 3D 'add nothing' has been softened to a scoped design decision for this 2D topic rather than a universal law.

probeDeeper: What would this fruit cost for 0 kg? Where must the line be at x = 0, and why?
How did you find the cost of 5 kg from the line — which way did you read, and how do you know it isn't, say, £, from the other axis?

Here is a line that is straight but does NOT go through the origin (a fixed £2 charge plus £2/kg) — is THAT one directly proportional? How can you tell? (counterexample separating 'straight' from 'proportional'.)
Show me this same relationship as a ratio table — where is the '×2' that the graph's steepness shows?
assess.correctAnswer: (a) 3 kg costs £6 (so this fruit is £2 per kg). (b) 5 kg costs £10 — read up from 5 on the x-axis to the line and across to £10. (c) A straight line through the origin passing through (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6)… — in fact the SAME line here, since £2/kg matches; if asked for, say £1/kg would be a shallower line through the origin, e.g. (3, 3).

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks any straight (or rising) line shows proportion; draws or accepts a line that misses the origin
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'what does this fruit cost for 0 kg?' — it must be £0, so the line has to start at the origin. Contrast with a fixed-charge line that misses it. Rehearse the origin test.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In (c) draws a line not through (0,0), or when shown a not-through-origin line calls it proportional

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the graph as isolated points and cannot interpolate an unknown, or swaps the axes
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model reading up from the x-value to the line and across to the y-axis; the line gives a value for EVERY weight, not just plotted ones. Label axes before reading.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 5 kg, only answers if 5 is a plotted point, or reads across-then-up the wrong way giving the wrong coordinate

errorPatterns.pattern: Does not connect the graph to the double number line / ratio table — treats them as unrelated
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put the three side by side for the same example; show the gradient, the column multiplier, and the number-line gap are the same number. Align the number line at 0.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Can read the graph but cannot say how the same relationship looks as a ratio table, or does not align the double number line at 0

responseLevels.gap: Misreads the axes or cannot interpolate; draws a line that misses the origin and treats any straight line as proportional.
responseLevels.full: Reads (3,6) as '3 kg for £6', interpolates 5 kg → £10 by reading the line, DRAWS a new proportional line through the origin, explains why it must pass through (0,0), and links the graph to the ratio table/double number line as the same constant multiplier.
responseLevels.partial: Interprets the given point and reads off 5 kg → £10 correctly, but draws a new line without anchoring it at the origin, or cannot translate the graph into a ratio table / double number line — recognition without full production or cross-representation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a graph: a straight line through the origin passing through the point (3, 6), where the x-axis is weight in kg and the y-axis is cost in pounds. (a) What does the point (3, 6) tell you? (b) Use the line to find the cost of 5 kg. (c) Now, on the same axes, DRAW the line for a different fruit that costs £2 per kg.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Interpreting a point, reading off an unknown, and then PRODUCING a proportional line all test whether the child sees the graph as a constant-multiplier relationship, not a picture. A child who has it reads (3,6) as '3 kg for £6', interpolates 5 kg → £10, and draws a new line THROUGH THE ORIGIN. A child who hasn't reads the axes the wrong way, cannot interpolate, or draws a line that misses (0,0). The 'now draw one' step is the discriminator — recognition alone won't produce a correct origin-anchored line.
